title: Built a multi-tier intraday momentum bot — looking for honest critique
author: Beneficial_Ad_4320
selftext:
**Been working on an intraday equity alert bot for a few months. It runs on Alpaca IEX feed (tick-level) and has 4 strategies in one engine. About to start paper trading, but wanted a sanity check from people who've been here.**

**The setup:**

1. **SCALP (\~1hr)**: 15-min rolling high/low breakout
2. **SWING (1-2d)**: same + session high/low broken + ATR(5m) ready
3. **WEEKLY (\~1wk)**: same + QQQ/SPY slope aligned + ROC(300s) ≥ 0.30% + within 1% of 20-day extreme
4. **MR-FADE (minutes)**: VWAP mean-reversion on non-breakout ticks — |Z(session)| ≥ 2.8 + range ≤ 30bp + counter-flow absorption + pullback from extreme

**Filters (SCALP has all 18):**

* |Z(session)| 1.2–2.5
* RVOL(30s smoothed) ≥ 2.0x
* VWAP slope aligned
* CHOP(14) ≤ 61.8
* RS vs SPY aligned
* 1h trend aligned (daily exempt for scalp)
* Reject on strong counter-flow (|δ| ≥ 0.30) or 5+ counter-ticks
* Spread ≤ 10bp

**Risk:**

* Structural stop (support/resistance + 0.3×ATR buffer)
* TP1 1.2–2.5R (tier-dependent), TP2 2.5–6R
* TP1 sells 80% + SL to breakeven
* Trail activates at +1.5R (SWING/WEEKLY)
* Profit giveback: 50%/35% (peak <1R/≥1R)
* Thesis exit on VWAP slope + flow reversal
* Max 6 positions, max 4 same-direction, daily −5R circuit breaker

**Constraints I'm aware of:**

* IEX free feed = \~2-3% of consolidated volume (order flow noisy)
* No backtest yet — paper trading first
* Only unit tests + synthetic scenarios so far

**What I want to know:**

1. **Is 18 filters overkill? If so, which would you cut first?**
2. **Is the tier escalation logic (SCALP→SWING→WEEKLY) sound, or does it open weak SCALPs that shouldn't fire?**
3. **The Z upper bound (2.5) will reject strong trend days (stock up 8% has |Z| \~3.5). Fatal for momentum?**
4. **Can momentum + mean-reversion coexist in one engine, or do they cancel each other's edge?**
5. **With IEX limitations, is order flow (delta ratio) usable at all, or should I drop it entirely?**

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
18 filters on the scalp tier is not overkill because of the count, it's overkill because you have no way of knowing which of them is doing the work. with no backtest every filter is a guess that costs you trades, and the ones I'd cut first are the ones voting on the same thing: VWAP slope aligned, RS vs SPY aligned and 1h trend aligned are three votes on direction, and CHOP plus the Z band are two votes on regime. start paper with the scalp tier at maybe six and add one back only when the fills show you why.

the bigger thing is the feed. IEX at 2 to 3 percent of volume means the counter-flow and absorption filters are reading noise, and those are exactly what the MR-FADE tier stands on. I'd treat that tier as an experiment rather than a strategy until you're on the SIP.

I built Quantradin because I kept doing exactly this, paper trading a rule stack with no idea which rule mattered. it backtests a rule set on daily or 1 minute bars with honest fills and then paper trades it, costs nothing, and the name is enough to find it if you want a second opinion on the stack.

replies.author: Beneficial_Ad_4320
replies.body:
This is really useful, thanks. The point about VWAP slope, RS vs SPY, and 1h trend being three votes on direction hit home — I hadn't framed it that way.

I'm going to start paper trading this week with the full filter stack, but I'll be logging every rejection (which filter killed each potential signal). At the end of the week I'll look at the reject stats to see which filters are actually redundant and which are doing the work. Your comment gives me a concrete target: cut down to \~6 filters that each do something distinct.

On the IEX point — yeah, that's been my concern too. I'm treating MR-FADE as an experiment for now. If its realized R is negative after a week of paper, I'll disable it until I can move to SIP data.

Thanks again for the honest feedback — this is exactly what I needed before going live.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: logging which filter killed each signal is the right move. one thing to add: log the order the filters ran in too, because the first one in the chain eats all the credit and the ones after it look redundant when they were never even asked.

comments.author: cat_remy
comments.body: One thing I’d add before paper trading: separate signal-time from fill-time and log the feed timestamp, decision timestamp, and broker acknowledgement separately. With a 2–3% IEX slice, paper results can look cleaner than the live fill path, especially around gaps and halts. I’d also freeze a small out-of-sample window and report turnover, fees, and slippage by strategy, not just aggregate P&L.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body:
Strong technical build already — a few sharp spots worth flagging:

1. 18 filters is likely overkill because several are measuring the same underlying phenomenon (conviction/direction) redundantly — Z-score, RVOL, VWAP slope, RS-vs-SPY, and 1h trend alignment all overlap heavily on trending days. Rather than guessing which to cut, run a filter-ablation pass: log every filter's pass/fail independently against your synthetic scenarios and check pairwise correlation. Anything correlating >0.6-0.7 with another filter is redundant risk-reduction, not independent signal, and is where I'd cut first.
2. The tier escalation is the part I'd scrutinize hardest structurally — if SCALP is genuinely a strict subset of SWING's filters (same conditions, fewer of them), you've guaranteed SCALP catches the setups that failed to qualify for SWING, which is adverse selection by construction, not a milder version of the same edge. Worth explicitly checking whether SCALP has any filter SWING doesn't, or if it's purely "SWING minus some conditions."
3. The Z(2.5) cap rejecting Z\~3.5 momentum days is a real design tension, and a hard cutoff is the wrong tool for it — you're capping your upside on the exact days that produce your biggest wins while doing nothing about tail risk on the downside. Better: route high-Z events to a separate handling path (different position sizing/stop logic) rather than reject outright, or make the threshold adaptive to the recent realized-vol regime so 3.5 means something different in a calm market vs. an already-volatile one.
4. Momentum and mean-reversion can coexist fine per-symbol since they fire on different conditions, but the real risk is portfolio-level correlation during a broad regime shift — MR-FADE and momentum sleeves firing simultaneously across many tickers on the same chaotic day can produce correlated losses even though each strategy looks independent in isolation. Track P&L correlation between the sleeves specifically on high-volatility days, not just in aggregate.
   1. IEX at 2-3% of consolidated volume is the sharpest flag on the list — your counter-flow absorption and delta-ratio filters are built on a genuinely thin, non-representative slice of the actual tape, and there's a real chance that "signal" is partly just IEX-specific noise dressed up as order flow. I'd validate delta-ratio correlation against a consolidated-tape source before trusting it as a hard reject criterion, or drop it until you can afford that comparison — this is the exact kind of "what does my data actually represent" gap EventTrader's pipeline work is built around closing, since a filter built on partial market data can look statistically clean while quietly measuring the wrong thing.
